newsitem.title: PERU: FEATURE-"Room with a view" in Peru fetches thousands.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-"Room with a view" in Peru fetches thousands.

text.p: At a school around the corner from the Japanese ambassador's house in Lima, children pray for the prompt and safe release of 72 hostages held at gunpoint by Marxist rebels.
But Elisa's prayer, in a whisper lest she be overheard by other third-graders, is different: "Dear God, forgive me, but don't let this end just yet."

Blushing, her mother explains: "We were able to pay a lot of debts thanks to Nestor Cerpa." Cerpa and 20-odd of his Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels have been holed up in the diplomat's mansion with the hostages since Dec. 17 to press for the release of 450 jailed comrades.

By renting rooms, apartments and rooftops to press photographers and cameramen mounting a round-the-clock vigil on the mansion in Lima's plush district of San Isidro, local residents are cashing in on the crisis.

Elisa's family has not only erased its debts by letting reporters use their 14th-floor apartment windows, they can now afford holidays in Miami and an $8,000 bash when Elisa's sister turns 15, limousine included.

On the down side, they have to share their house, which they now call "the labyrinth," with reporters who tramp in and out day and night. For good measure, a police sharpshooter often spends nights in their kitchen, training his rifle on the mansion. And that does not bring in any revenue.
RENTS CHALLENGE MANHATTAN HIGHS
Rent rates vary depending on space, angle and location from $500 a week for a room with a window facing the residence to $1,500 for a three-bedroom apartment on a 15th floor.
"We're paying $6,000 a month and the owner keeps asking for more," complained a reporter from Tokyos's Nikkei financial newspaper. Not bad for an apartment that sells for $80,000.

Space on a tall building's roof costs about $1,000 a week. Major Japanese and international TV stations have set up plastic tents and mount constant guard over the mansion, using infrared lenses at night.

Most of the time all they can see is Red Cross members carrying in food and medicines, mediators arriving for talks with Cerpa or hostages having dinner by candlelight since the government cut off electricity, water and telephone lines.

But some nights the rebels will scamper onto the roof of the house, a 20-by-30-yard (metre) colonial-style mansion sorrounded by now-mined and booby-trapped gardens, to unfurl a new banner promoting their cause. Cameras start rolling and clicking.

The media-conscious rebels then call TV reporters on walkie-talkies. "Do you see the banner, man?" one asked recently. "Not very well, a tree is on the way. Move it a little to the right," came the answer.
The rebels promptly went out and moved the banner. And in the morning they chopped down the tree.
Although most of the 500 hostages were freed in the first few weeks, 72 men, including two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen, still remain captive.
A GOLD POT FOR A RAINY DAY

One of the buildings in the area is housing five TV stations on the roof, for a total of $5,000 a week, plus another five in a hallway paying an extra $2,500. That is $30,000 a month, or some $100,000 for the condominium fund since the siege started.

"We will be able to fix the elevators and pipes, buy a generator to have electricity during blackouts, and contract insurance," the building's accountant said. Any money left will go to a rainy-day fund.

With a strong interest in the story and an even stronger yen, Japanese reporters are the most sought-after by residents looking for temporary tenants. Nikkei, for example, has dispatched 14 reporters, although they plan to cut manpower by half now that talks to solve the crisis have stalled.

They and media from Peru and other countries are not only renting space but also providing temporary work to an army of free-lance reporters, drivers and translators. The translators, mostly young members of the 80,000-strong Japanese-Peruvian community, make $120 a day listening to radios, reading mewspapers and helping Japanese reporters communicate with local officials.
SPIRITUAL HEALING, SOUL SAVING ARE FREE

One pastry shop down the street from the residence decided to close its doors for security reasons but it rented its terrace to a Japanese TV station, which has set up its crisis headquarters under the shop's canvas. Others seeking to make a profit out of the crisis include hotels in the area, which have marked up their rates, and street vendors of all sorts.
"Hi, what is your name? I am Sofia. It's hot in here, isn't it?" a young woman used to say as soon as the sun set, before she was chased away by the police.
Not all are in for the money, though. Witch doctors, shamans and members of assorted cults have turned up offering spiritual healing and soul salvation free of charge.

And fortune of a different kind shone on a Peruvian cameraman and an American TV producer who met during the crisis. It was love at first sight followed by wedlock at the nearby district of Miraflores.
As luck would have it, the wedding was performed by the mayor of Miraflores -- a former MRTA hostage.
